analysis.one_liner: Sets the annual Pentagon budget and delivers pay raises, health coverage, and survivor benefits for service members and veterans.
analysis.headline: The annual defense bill became Public Law 108-375 on October 28, 2004, after the House passed it 391-34 and the Senate approved it by unanimous consent.
analysis.plain_summary: This is the yearly bill that authorizes what the Defense Department may spend in fiscal year 2005: weapons procurement, research, operations, and military construction. It also raises military pay by 3.5 percent, expands health coverage for activated reservists and their families, improves survivor benefits for military widows and widowers, and compensates nuclear weapons workers sickened on the job. Along the way it hands out major contracts to defense contractors, including authority for a multiyear purchase of up to 100 refueling tanker aircraft to replace a leasing arrangement tainted by scandal.
analysis.who_benefits: Military members and their families gain a 3.5 percent pay raise, permanent increases in imminent-danger pay and family separation allowances, permanent TRICARE health coverage tied to reserve mobilizations, a phased increase in survivor annuities from 35 to 55 percent, and immediate full concurrent receipt of retired pay and disability compensation for veterans rated 100 percent disabled. Defense contractors gain tens of billions in authorized procurement, including the tanker multiyear buy and shipbuilding programs. Federal civilian workers gain new protest rights and cost thresholds in public-private job competitions, and sickened nuclear facility workers gain a new federal compensation program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Service members, military families, veterans, defense contractors

how_it_helps.text: Raises military basic pay by 3.5 percent effective January 1, 2005, and makes permanent the increases in imminent danger pay (from $150 to $225 monthly) and the family separation allowance (from $100 to $250 monthly).

Makes permanent early TRICARE eligibility for reservists with delayed-effective mobilization orders, lets the Secretary waive deductibles for activated reservists' dependents, extends transitional health care after separation from 120 to 180 days, and creates a premium-based TRICARE option for reservists who commit to continued service after a mobilization.

Phases out the two-tier annuity for Survivor Benefit Plan recipients over 62, raising payments from 35 percent toward 55 percent of retired pay, and repeals the phase-in of concurrent receipt so retirees rated 100 percent disabled receive both retired pay and disability compensation immediately.

Ends the Air Force tanker lease arrangement and authorizes a multiyear procurement of up to 100 aerial refueling aircraft, following the Boeing tanker leasing scandal, and states that anyone involved in improper activities tied to the program should be investigated and prosecuted.

Expands the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program so Department of Energy contractor employees sickened by toxic exposure at nuclear facilities can receive federal compensation, with an ombudsman in the Labor Department to help them file claims.

Protects federal civilian employees in public-private job competitions by requiring formal cost comparisons, preserving civilian performance unless contracting saves at least $10 million or 10 percent, and giving federal employees bid-protest rights under OMB Circular A-76.

Directs the Defense Department to develop a comprehensive sexual assault prevention and response policy, extends the task force examining sexual assault in the military, and requires review of the military justice system's handling of sexual offenses.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost: the bill authorizes the full fiscal year 2005 defense budget across procurement, research, operations, personnel, and military construction, plus additional authorizations for operations in Iraq and Afghanistan. Taxpayers also fund the expanded health, survivor, and worker-compensation benefits through the Treasury, including a shift of military retiree health fund payments to the general fund starting in fiscal 2006.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes the entire annual defense budget with broad bipartisan support, including large procurement programs, leaving little external check on the cost of weapons systems; it adds rapid-acquisition authority allowing up to $100 million per year in emergency purchases with a 15-day contract goal, and raises the threshold for senior approval of noncompetitive procurement procedures from $50 million to $75 million.

The Senate had attached a hate crimes title (the Local Law Enforcement Enhancement Act) and broadcast decency provisions to the bill, and the House voted 213-186 to instruct conferees to accept the hate crimes provisions, but the conference report dropped both; the final law contains no hate crimes title.
The law makes Freedom of Information Act disclosure requirements inapplicable to land remote sensing information collected by the United States and provided to state or local governments.

Many of the personnel and benefit provisions are studies, reports, or pilot programs rather than binding guarantees, and several benefit expansions carry caps or recoupment requirements, such as limits on bonus funding and repayment of advances for members in combat zones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For service members, reservists, and veterans the bill delivers substantial, concrete gains: higher pay and combat allowances, durable health coverage around mobilizations, and long-sought fixes to survivor and disability benefits. For taxpayers the bill is the annual cost of national defense writ large, and its procurement side tilts toward contractors with looser competition requirements and emergency purchasing authority; the strongest criticism from the record is that broadly supported Senate riders on hate crimes and broadcast decency were stripped in conference while the defense and contracting provisions sailed through.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 391-34, the Senate passed its own version by unanimous consent, a conference committee merged the two, both chambers approved the merger (the House 359-14, the Senate by unanimous consent), and President Bush signed it into law on October 28, 2004 as Public Law 108-375.

narrative.text: Introduced April 22, 2004 by Representative Duncan Hunter and referred to the Armed Services Committee, which held extensive hearings and reported the bill 60-0 on May 14, 2004.

The House passed the bill 391-34 on May 20, 2004, with 169 of 205 voting Democrats, 221 of 228 voting Republicans, and the lone Independent in favor; a Democratic motion to recommit failed 202-224 on a near party-line vote.
On June 23, 2004 the Senate passed its own version by unanimous consent, adding non-defense titles including hate crimes enforcement and broadcast decency penalties.

On September 28, 2004 the House voted 213-186 to instruct its conferees to accept the Senate's hate crimes title, with 182 of 205 voting Democrats in favor and 177 of 226 voting Republicans opposed, but the conference report filed October 8 dropped the hate crimes title.
The House adopted the conference report 359-14 on October 9, 2004, the Senate agreed by unanimous consent the same day, and the President signed it October 28, 2004.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Military members, reservists, and veterans gained the pay, health, and survivor benefit improvements, and defense contractors gained authorized procurement including the 100-aircraft tanker buy. Opponents of the Senate's hate crimes and broadcast decency riders also came out ahead, since conferees stripped both from the final law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Military families, contractors, and foes of the dropped riders

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was overwhelming in both parties (House 391-34 with 221 of 228 voting Republicans and 169 of 205 voting Democrats in favor; the Senate passed by unanimous consent), though the fight over the stripped hate crimes rider split largely by party, 213-186.

industries.note: The bill authorizes the annual flow of procurement, research, and operations money that is the defense industry's core revenue, including multiyear buys and extended pilot programs for Army industrial facilities, while adding some cost and competition disclosures. Contractors remain the permanent channel through which defense goods and services are purchased.

The law ends the scandal-plagued tanker lease and authorizes a multiyear purchase of up to 100 aerial refueling aircraft, with outside-panel review required before contract award — a large new order paired with extra oversight.
The bill funds destroyer modernization, authorizes the first LHA(R) amphibious assault ship, and supports shipbuilding cost-reduction research; the work sustains jobs in shipyard communities.

The law extends authority for contractor-performed security-guard functions and requires Defense Department guidance on managing contractors supporting deployed forces, while bringing contractor interrogation and security personnel under reporting, training, and extraterritorial jurisdiction requirements.

Activated reservists and separating members gain longer TRICARE coverage, which shifts some customers to the military system and away from private employer plans, but the law also studies stipends for keeping private coverage and lets providers bill the government additional amounts for reservists' dependents.

The law reauthorizes and expands FEMA firefighter assistance grants, extends them to non-hospital emergency medical services organizations, reduces matching requirements for small communities, and directs aerial firefighting aircraft purchases.

Public-private job competitions gained new protest rights and cost-comparison protections that keep work with federal employees unless contracting saves significantly, but the law also extends contractor security-guard authority and pilots municipal service purchases.
